newsitem.title: USA: Weekly jobless claims down last week.
newsitem.headline: Weekly jobless claims down last week.

text.p: Fewer Americans waited on unemployment lines to collect jobless benefits last week, the government said on Thursday, providing more proof of a strong labour market and a steadily expanding economy.

The Labour Department said new claims for state unemployment benefits in the week ended March 1 dipped to 310,000, from 316,000 in the previous week. Wall Street economists had expected initial jobless claims of 317,000.
A key gauge of jobless trends -- the department's four-week moving average -- continued a descent that began at the start of 1997, falling to its lowest level last week in nearly eight years.
Economists monitor the average closely as a more reliable indicator than the individual weekly figure because it smooths out weekly blips and helps to reveal trends in the data.
Last week, the average stood at 310,000, down from 313,500 the previous week. It was the lowest it has been since it reached 309,750 in the week ended May 13, 1989, the department said.
Economists noted that a healthy labour market and low unemployment rates are linked closely with just how secure consumers feel about their economic well-being.
"It's a sign of a very strong economy," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc. in St. Louis. "This is consistent with the high levels of consumer confidence we're seeing."

The report follows a string of data showing a buoyant mood on the part of consumers. Most recently, the government said consumers boosted their spending in January as incomes kept rising. Sales of both new and existing homes also have been on the upswing in early 1997.
Just last week, a closely watched report revealed that consumer confidence continued to ride high in February and will likely remain strong in the year ahead.
The latest weekly jobless claims activity will not be reflected in Friday's employment report for February because the monthly survey is conducted near the middle of the month.
But economists said the steadily declining four-week average of initial claims suggests that labour conditions will continue to become tighter.
"These strong numbers confirm that the strong trend going into tomorrow's report is actually valid," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors in Columbus, Ohio.
The moving average generally tends to rise in February, Chan said, suggesting that the average's big drop this February cannot be linked solely to seasonal factors.
Economists noted that the firm labour market conditions reported so far help explain recent warnings by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
The Fed chief told Congress that the Fed might decide to raise interest rates before inflation picks up to ensure that the nearly six-year-old economic expansion continues at a steady pace.
A.G. Edwards' Thayer said the jobless claims data are "consistent" with Greenspan's cautionary remarks about inflation.
